why: The policy says requirements are derived yearly from the business plan, contracts and law and kept in a security requirements list, but that list is not in the evidence.
Policy 4.0 is signed by both managing directors and the record confirms management approval on 14 July 2026.
The policy's Purpose and Objectives sections state why security matters and set concrete objectives.
An intranet export shows all ten policies published under Security, viewed by 163 of 171 employees.
Four change notices in 2026 went to all employees and, where relevant, to suppliers through the supplier portal.
Requirements are derived from the business plan, customer contract clauses and German law including data protection.
No document states consequences for non-conformance with the policies.
Nine supporting standards and procedures exist, each with an owner, and are published.
Review cycles are defined and the main policy was reviewed in July 2026, but the encryption standard (yearly cycle) has not been reviewed since March 2022.
The procedure's examples cover personnel, physical, IT and supplier events, and it is published, on posters and in the yearly training taken by 97 percent of staff.
Email, ticket and hotline channels are defined and the register shows 43 reports received through them in 2026.
The security desk feeds back within two working days and the register confirms every reporter received feedback.
The security desk is named as the single point of contact for all reports.
Urgent events go to a staffed hotline with on-call forwarding, others by email or ticket; both channels were used in 2026.
The reporting duty is in the employment contract and covered by the yearly training, with completion recorded.
A supplier report was received and acted on the same day, but no channel is shown as communicated to external parties.
Contact details are on the intranet start page and on a poster next to every time clock, reaching office and production staff.
A two-working-day feedback rule exists and the register records feedback dates for every entry.
Every report was recorded within one working day and the median time to first action was three hours.
Register entries show proportionate actions such as password resets, door repair, USB port blocking and supplier file checks.
A post-incident review is required and a briefing followed the phishing incident, but no review has been recorded for the two high and critical incidents.
Reports are sorted by category, type and priority, as the register entries show.
Owners per category, cross-area coordination, deputies and escalation of critical reports are defined, but qualification and resources are not addressed.
No document covers reporting criminal aspects of incidents to authorities.
The 2026 basic course was completed by 166 of 171 employees, with the rest scheduled on return from leave.
The concept covers policy, reporting, malware, login rules, NDAs and external IT services, but not compliance issues of information security.
Administrators, managers and staff on customer networks or in prototype areas get target-group sessions.
Management approved the concept on 16 February 2026.
A yearly course ran in Q1 2026 and a briefing was sent after the phishing incident.
An e-learning export and session attendance tables document participation.
The information security officer and security desk are named in every course, on the intranet and on posters.
Sign-in methods are chosen by exposure, with a second factor for internet-facing systems, and the rollout record shows this applied per system.
12-character minimum, breach-list check, no forced expiry, app second factor and hardware keys follow national authority guidance and are configured.
Procedures are defined by system exposure and enforced in the directory and on internet-facing systems.
Directory settings enforce 12 characters, breached-password blocking and lockout after failed attempts.
All nine administrator accounts are separate and require a hardware security key since April 2026.
Joiner, mover and leaver tickets in 2026 show accounts created, changed, disabled and deleted per the procedure.
One named account per person is the rule and the review confirmed every employee account belongs to a current employee.
Shared accounts are limited to read-only production display terminals, each registered with a reason and responsible manager.
All nine 2026 leaver accounts were disabled by the end of the last working day, with timestamps in the sample.
Six-monthly reviews are required and the H1 2026 review, following one in January 2026, is recorded.
The procedure requires starting passwords in person or by text with a forced change, but no record shows this being done.
The rules cover non-disclosure, no writing down, change on suspicion, no private reuse, change at first sign-in and password quality, with directory settings enforcing quality.
New accounts start with a standard employee role limited to email, intranet and office software, as the joiner tickets show.
No document addresses manufacturer default accounts or passwords.
Every joiner account was approved by the system owner before creation.
A manager requests and the system owner approves, and the tickets show both parties.
End dates are required, but the review found three supplier accounts still active after their jobs had ended.
Disabling by the last working day and deletion after 90 days are defined and shown applied.
No evidence of a technical control preventing default passwords.
Authenticator apps and hardware keys are in use, but nothing covers securing the medium itself, such as enrolment or loss.
Internal accounts are reviewed six-monthly, but accounts in customers' systems were excluded from the review.
No document addresses interactive login for technical accounts.
Request, approval, least privilege and revocation are defined and the tickets and review show them applied.
Employee, administrator, supplier and technical rights were reviewed in H1 2026, but customer IT systems were out of scope.
The policy sets a start-from-nothing, job-based authorisation strategy.
Rights are bundled into 14 owned roles, which were reviewed in June 2026.
Rights follow the job's role and unneeded rights are refused, as the ticket sample shows.
Ordinary accounts never hold admin rights and all nine admin accounts are separate.
A mover's old role was removed the same day, but the review found 11 rights left over from earlier role changes.
AES-256, TLS 1.2+ and authority-recommended algorithms are set and TLS was tested, but the encryption standard is four years past its yearly review.
Methods and key strengths are defined but the key lifecycle omits archiving, retrieval, distribution and deletion, and the standard is overdue for review.
Registers list the three in-house transfer services and the three approved outside services.
Rules per classification are defined and each service's highest allowed classification is registered.
TLS 1.2+ is enforced and was verified by an external scan in September 2026; the platform also encrypts at rest.
No measure for ensuring correct addressing or correct transfer is described.
Transport encryption on all services and end-to-end or platform encryption for confidential data are defined and verified.
Logging requirements, retention and works council agreement are defined and the scope list and reviews show them in use.
Sign-ins, account changes and administrator actions are logged on every in-scope system.
A logging scope list, checked in March 2026, records each system's need for logging.
The providers' monitoring options are documented, but the register states nobody considered or watches them.
Monthly log reviews from June to September 2026 are recorded with findings.
Log findings go to the security desk and two were passed on as register entries.
Logs go to a central server that other administrators cannot change or delete.
Logging covers system sign-ins and changes, with no monitoring of network-level actions.
Advisories are gathered nightly from manufacturers and the CVE database and scored with CVSS 3.1.
Each CVE lists affected assets and a priority.
Each vulnerability has a patch ticket, a scheduled update or a documented risk acceptance; one medium item is three days overdue with a rescheduling decision.
Patch tickets and maintenance windows are used, but no patch management process covering testing is documented.
The unpatchable CAD vault server is restricted to the design VLAN with logged downloads until replacement.
Patch tickets are recorded as closed, but no verification of successful installation is shown.
No backup concept is in the evidence.
No recovery concept is in the evidence; the policy's one-day recovery objective is not a concept.
No per-service backup and recovery concept or recovery sequence is documented.
